<b>How the Imami critics judge</b> — on: How the Imami critics judge — on two axes: reliability (thiqa; praised — jalil, wajh, 'ayn, la ba's bihi; weak) and creed (Imami, or Waqifi, Fathi, Zaydi, 'ammi …). Together they give the classical four: an Imami thiqa, a praised narrator (mamduh), a thiqa of another school (muwaththaq), a weak one. Read from the critic's own words at the head of the entry; a creed he does not state is left unknown. Not Ibn Hajar's scale: each tradition is shown by its own measure.
<b>Rank</b> — Ibn Hajar sorts narrators: Rank — Ibn Hajar sorts narrators into twelve degrees, from the Companions (1) down to the accused liar (12); 2–3 are trustworthy, 4 truthful, 5–6 acceptable, 7–12 weak to rejected. Tabaqa — the generation: 1 Companions, 2–5 Successors, 6–9 their followers, 10–12 the compilers' teachers.

The table asks another question: even when they rank the hadith alike, does one give stronger grades overall? The hadith model (an ordinal, proportion: The hadith model (an ordinal, proportional-odds regression) gives each factor ONE weight for every step of the grades — from sahih to hasan as from hasan to da'if. Brant's test fits each step on its own and asks whether the weights differ beyond chance (Wald χ², Holm-adjusted over the factors). Where they do, the odds ratios at each step show how: a factor that weighs more at the later step decides between hasan and da'if more than between sahih and hasan. The model's odds ratio is then an average of the steps, still telling the direction. A step a factor never reaches cannot be estimated and is left out.
